question: How do we check whether a shuttle has the right speed?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing: how to check whether a shuttle has the right speed. I split it into the two sub-parts the rule book itself uses: (1) how the test stroke must be played — Law 3.1 sentences (1) and (2) state the full underhand stroke contacting the shuttle over the back boundary line, hit at an upward angle parallel to the side lines; (2) what result shows correct speed — Law 3.2 sentence (1) states the shuttle must land not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line (Diagram B). Both parts are answered by the Laws of Badminton, so no further searching is needed. The ITTO clauses about the referee testing all speeds from both ends (itto-3.5.4.2) and assessing how the shuttle was hit (itto-3.5.4.4) bear on the topic without answering the question, so they go in related_sentences.
answer.answer: To test a shuttle for speed, a player shall use a full underhand stroke which makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line [1], and the shuttle shall be hit at an upward angle and in a direction parallel to the side lines [2]. A shuttle has the correct speed when it lands not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line [3]. All available speeds shall be tested from both ends of the court [4]. When assessing the result of the shuttle test, take into account the manner in which the shuttles were hit, including the strength of shot and trajectory, and whether they were hit from the correct location over the back line [5].

citations.quote: To test a shuttle, a player shall use a full underhand stroke which makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line.
The shuttle shall be hit at an upward angle and in a direction parallel to the side lines.
A shuttle of correct speed will land not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line as in Diagram B.
All available speeds shall be tested from both ends of the court.

When assessing the result of the shuttle test, take into account the manner in which the shuttles were hit (strength of shot and trajectory), and whether they were hit from the correct location (over the back line) (Law 3).

question: How wide are the court lines, and what's the call when a shuttle lands on a line?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts. (1) The width of the court lines: Laws of Badminton Clause 1.1, sentence (1) states the court is marked out with lines 40 mm wide — laws-1.1 (1). No Alternative Laws variant for line width appeared in search, so the standard Laws sentence suffices. (2) The call when a shuttle lands on a line: Laws Clause 13.3.1 sentences (1)–(2) state a fault occurs only when the shuttle lands outside the boundaries, i.e. 'not on or within the boundary lines' — so landing on a line is in, not a fault (laws-13.3.1 (1), (2)). The officiating call is covered by ITTO 5.8.3.1 (1) ('Out' only when the shuttle lands outside the line) and ITTO 8.4 (1) (if the shuttle lands in, the Line Judge says nothing but points to the line). Related but not directly answering: laws-17.4 (1) (line judge indicates 'in' or 'out' on assigned lines) and itto-8.3 (1) (the 'Out' call when the shuttle lands out).
answer.answer: The court shall be a rectangle marked out with lines 40 mm wide [1]. A shuttle that lands on a line is in, not out, because a shuttle is out only when it lands outside the boundaries of the court, that is, not on or within the boundary lines [2][3]. The call is therefore not "Out": "Out" is called when the shuttle lands outside the line [4], and when it lands out the Line Judge calls "Out" promptly in a clear voice loud enough to be heard by the players and the spectators while extending both arms horizontally [7]. When the shuttle lands in, the Line Judge says nothing but points to the line with the right hand while looking towards the Umpire [5], thereby indicating that the shuttle landed 'in' on the line assigned [6].

question: What am I allowed to attach to my racket?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: 'The sources do not say what you are allowed to attach to your racket.' Law 4.3.1(1) answers it directly: the racket shall be free of attached objects and protrusions other than those used solely and specifically to limit/prevent wear and tear, or vibration, or to distribute weight, or to secure the handle by cord to the player's hand, and which are reasonable in size and placement for such purposes. Law 4.3.2(1) is the nearest related prohibition (no device that materially changes the racket's shape), so it goes in related_sentences. The Alternative Laws only replace service laws (alt-alternative-service:intro), so no alternative-format racket rule exists; standard Law 4.3 applies everywhere.
answer.answer: You may attach objects or protrusions to your racket only when they are used solely and specifically to limit or prevent wear and tear, or vibration, or to distribute weight, or to secure the handle by cord to your hand, and they are reasonable in size and placement for those purposes [1]. You may not attach any device that makes it possible for you to change materially the shape of the racket [2].

question: What's the minimum rest a player gets between two matches?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing: the minimum rest a player is entitled to between two matches. The Instructions to Technical Officials clause 3.5.17.4 answers it directly: sentence (1) gives the standard minimum of a 60-minute interval between matches, reducible by the Referee in exceptional circumstances to no less than 30 minutes; sentence (2) gives the 30-minute minimum for junior, junior team, Para badminton tournaments and qualifying rounds; sentence (3) says the Referee should try to provide a longer interval. Law 16.2 (laws-16.2.1/16.2.2) covers intervals within a match (between games), not between matches, so it does not answer this part; itto-3.5.17.5 (avoiding disproportionately different rest times) bears on the topic without answering it, so it goes in related_sentences.
answer.answer: A player is entitled to a minimum 60-minute interval between two matches, and in exceptional circumstances the Referee can reduce that interval to no less than 30 minutes [1]. In Junior tournaments, Junior team tournaments, Para badminton tournaments, and qualifying rounds of other tournaments, in force 2025-04-26, the player is entitled to a minimum 30-minute interval between two matches [2]. The Referee shall try to provide a longer interval between any two matches of a given player, and in particular between that player's matches in the same event [3]. Opposing sides in a match should not have disproportionately different rest times since their previous round matches in that event [4].

citations.quote: Any player is entitled to a minimum of a 60-minute interval between matches, or in exceptional circumstances, the Referee can reduce the interval to no less than 30 minutes between two matches (GCR, Regulation 11.3).

In Junior tournaments, Junior team tournaments, Para badminton tournaments, and qualifying rounds of other tournaments the player is entitled to a minimum of a 30-minute minimum interval between two matches.
The Referee shall, however, try to provide a longer interval between any two matches of a given player, and in particular between a player’s matches in the same event.
Ensure that opposing sides in a match do not have disproportionately different rest times since their previous round matches in that event.

question: The cork came off the shuttle in the middle of a rally. What happens?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing in three aspects: what happens when the cork/base separates from the shuttle mid-rally, who calls it, and what happens to the rally afterwards. Law 14.1(1) states 'let' is called by the umpire (or a player if no umpire) to halt play. Law 14.3(1) states that when a let occurs, play since the last service does not count and the last server serves again. Law 15.3(1) (shuttle not in play when a let has occurred) bears on the question without answering a part, so it goes in related_sentences.

question: My string broke during a rally. What am I allowed to do about my racket?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what a player may do about their racket when a string breaks during a rally. Parts: (1) whether a racket change at courtside during a rally is permitted — answered by ITTO 5.10.1 (2): "A change of a racket at courtside during a rally is permitted." (2) the conditions/limits on doing so — ITTO 5.10.1 (1) (players do not leave the court without the umpire's permission except in Law 16.2 intervals, or without delaying play), Law 16.5.2 (1) (no leaving the court during a match without the umpire's permission, causing delay), Law 16.4.1 (1) (play shall not be delayed), Law 16.4.2 (1) (umpire is sole judge of delay), and ITTO 5.11.1 (2) (testing of replacement rackets on court shall be prevented). (3) whether a broken string makes the rally a let or entitles a replay — searched the Laws (Law 14.2 lets list, Law 13 faults, Law 15) and the ITTO; no sentence addresses a broken string as a let or fault, so this part has no sentences; the nearest rule is Law 14.2.7 (1) on unforeseen or accidental situations, placed in related_sentences.
answer.answer: You may change your racket at courtside during the rally [1]. If you leave the court during the rally you need the umpire's permission and must not delay play [2][3]. Play must not be delayed to recover strength or wind or to receive advice [4], and the umpire is the sole judge of any delay in play [5]. You must not test a replacement racket on court, and the umpire shall prevent it [6]. The rules given do not say whether a broken string during a rally is a 'let' or otherwise entitles you to a replay of the rally.

No player shall leave the court during a match without the umpire’s permission, causing delay to play, except during the intervals as described in Law 16.2.
Under no circumstances shall play be delayed to enable a player to recover strength or wind or to receive advice.
The umpire shall be the sole judge of any delay in play.
Any unnecessary walk around the court between rallies and testing of replacement rackets on court, shall be prevented and if necessary, Law 16.7 shall be applied.

question: What does a black card mean, and who decides to give it?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what a black card means, and (2) who decides to give it. The Laws of Badminton do not use the words "black card"; Law 16.7.2 (laws-16.7.2, sentence 1) states that on faulting a side the umpire reports to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match. The Instructions to Technical Officials define the black card's use: itto-5.17.5 sentence 1 says that when the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair, a black card is given to the Umpire; sentences 3 and 4 say the Umpire then calls the player(s) "disqualified for misconduct" with an explanation while raising the black card above the head. So the black card means disqualification for misconduct (itto-5.17.5 sentences 1, 3, 4; laws-16.7.2 sentence 1), and the Referee is the one who decides (itto-5.17.5 sentence 1; laws-16.7.2 sentence 1). A search for "black card" confirmed no other clause defines it. Related: itto-5.17.10 sentence 2 notes cards given before the match have no effect on the score.
answer.answer: A black card means that the offending player or pair is disqualified for misconduct [1][2], and the Referee decides to give it [1][4]. When the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair of players, a black card is given to the Umpire [1], who then says "Come here" to the offending player or pair followed by "[name of player(s)], disqualified for misconduct" and a specific explanation of the misconduct [2], while at the same time raising the right hand holding the black card above the Umpire's head [3]. On faulting a side, the umpire reports the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match [4]. Any card given has no effect on the score of the match, but it is taken into account if further offences occur during the match [5].

question: What colour does a shuttle have to be?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: the colour a shuttle has to be. I searched the rule books repeatedly (shuttle colour, white or yellow, shuttlecock colour, Law 2.5, equipment compliance, para and alternative laws). Law 2 (SHUTTLE) in the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) covers only materials and flight characteristics (2.1), feathered-shuttle specs (2.2.1–2.2.6), non-feathered specs (2.3.1–2.3.3), and approved modifications for altitude/climate (2.4) — none states a colour. The only 'white or yellow' clause in the Laws is Law 1.2, which applies to court lines, not the shuttle. The Alternative Laws cover only service and scoring, and the ITTO mentions shuttle speed testing and change of shuttle but never colour. Law 5.1 says BWF rules on whether a shuttle complies with the specifications, but no sentence in any source states what colour a shuttle must be. So the single part has no answering sentence; the nearest shuttle rules go in related_sentences.
answer.answer:
The sources do not say the colour a shuttle has to be.
Related (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 2.1): "The shuttle shall be made of natural and / or synthetic materials."
Related (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 2.1): "From whatever material the shuttle is made, the flight characteristics generally shall be similar to those produced by a natural feathered shuttle with a cork base covered by a thin layer of leather."
Related (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 2.4): "Subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, modifications in the above specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable."
Related (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 5.1): "Compliance The Badminton World Federation shall rule on any question of whether any racket, shuttle or equipment or any prototype used in the playing of Badminton complies with the specifications."
